_comment: Canonical Game Guide content for Defenders of the Realm: Echoes of Elarion. Authored content for the in-game opt-in help codex (WO-588). The guide panel (GuideVM + View) renders whatever sections this file declares: tabs down the left, body + tips on the right. Adding or editing a section is a DATA change, no code. Each section is grounded in the SHIPPED game; any not-yet-built system is marked status 'coming' rather than described as live. Building entries are enumerated one-per-real-building from Assets/Resources/Data/Canonical/buildings.json (plus the Heart of Elarion, the village's central structure). Display names follow canon-strings.json. Tone: warm, concise, encouraging. HEARTFIRE PASS 2026-09-05 (WO-1415): added the 'heartfire' section. It had ZERO mentions here while being the ONE gate on raiding (WO-1379), which is the copy gap the owner found in felt-test. The ruled sentence 'each one sends you on a raid' is shared verbatim with the introduction beat and HeartfireCharges.SpendSentence. FRESHNESS PASS 2026-08-02: corrected the Echo roster cap (6, not 4), dropped the unbuilt silo-upgrade promise, retired the old 'hold the last light' tagline line, and added echo_affinity / echo_synergy / work_queue / raids / dungeons / saves_signin. Player-facing naming law: the timed-work system is called the Work Queue with Builders / Training / Research channels -- never 'Obsidian' (ObsidianQueueHud.cs). The GLOSSARY tabs are NOT in this file: they are appended by GuideVM from glossary.json (same Canonical folder).

sections.title: Basic Mechanics
body: You play one hero, the Keeper of Elarion, and you control only the Keeper. Everything else in the realm acts on its own, so you are never juggling a squad. Walk with WASD, the arrow keys, a gamepad stick, or the on-screen joystick on touch and web builds. The camera follows you while you explore.

The loop is simple and it always comes home: leave the hub to explore and fight, win resources and gear, then return to grow the village and your hero. Push the dark back and the realm heals a little more each time.
Approach a person, gate, building, or glowing object and an interact prompt appears. That single button opens dialogue, shops, the build menu, or a region crossing depending on what you are facing.
tips: Movement is camera-relative: push the stick where you want to go on screen.
Most panels share one Close button, top of the frame. There is no clutter of X buttons.
Nothing here is timed against you out in the world. Take your time and read.
Open this guide any time from Settings; it never blocks play.

sections.title: Objectives
body: Your current goal is always one glance away. The Quest Tracker card on the right edge of the screen shows the quest you are following and the exact step in front of you, like 'Speak with the Village Elder' or 'Clear the outpost.'

Objectives advance as you do the thing they ask. Finish a step and the card updates to the next one; finish the last step and the quest completes and pays out. You never have to guess what to do next.
Tap the tracker card to open the full quest log and see everything you have available, active, and completed.
tips: If you ever feel lost, read the tracker card first.
The Heart of Elarion also speaks as danger rises during a defense, a living cue that something needs you.
Completed objectives often unlock the next building, region, or hero ability.

sections.title: Quests
body: Quests are how the story of Elarion unfolds and how you earn many of your rewards. You pick them up by talking to people in the village and the world. Each quest runs through a chain of stages, and each stage has a clear objective and a reward when you clear it.

There are story quests that carry the main tale, gear quests that lead you toward better equipment, and side quests for extra resources. The Quest Tracker follows one at a time; the quest log lists them all with their progress.

Conversations use a clean dialogue box, one speaker and their line at a time, with choices when they matter. Some options only appear once you have done the right thing or hold the right item, so coming back to a character later can open new threads.
tips: Rewards can be resources (Crystals, Wood, Iron, Stone) or a granted item.
Some stages grant a keystone that feeds your hero progression, so they are worth chasing.
Revisit villagers after big events; their dialogue and offers change.

sections.title: Exploration
body: Home is the castle hub, with the Outer World streaming in around it so you can walk straight out into the realm. The world is built as connected regions joined by natural, diegetic crossings, a bridge, a tunnel, a mountain pass, rather than invisible walls.

These crossings are Region Gates. Walk up to one, step onto the threshold, and the gate carries you across the seam into the next region. Some warp you, some stream the next area in around you, but they always read as a real place you walk through.

Out in the world you will find enemy outposts and wandering threats. Closing on one starts a battle. Clearing them pushes the darkness back, which strengthens the world tree and speeds your Echoes' harvest, so exploring is never just sightseeing.
tips: Crossings are safe to walk up to; the transition only triggers on the threshold.
Clearing the world is permanent progress, not just one-time loot.
Watch for glowing nodes and collectibles tucked into the regions.

sections.title: Inventory
body: The Inventory is where you view and equip everything you own. It is laid out as tabs over a grid: Weapons, Armor, Accessories, and Consumables. Tap any item to see its stats and the actions you can take, Equip, Use, or Drop.
Beside the grid, a live 3D preview of your hero, the Gear Preview, shows exactly how your current loadout looks. Change a piece and the hero updates in place, so you always see what you are wearing.

Your hero has five equip slots: Main Hand for your weapon, Off-Hand for a shield, an Armor set, a Ring, and an Amulet. The Off-Hand only accepts shields, so a sword and shield stay clearly delineated from a two-handed grip.
tips: Equipped pieces are marked on the grid so you can see your set at a glance.
The detail strip shows stat changes before you commit to a swap.
Off-Hand is shields only; weapons go in the Main Hand.
Consumables are used straight from the inventory.

sections.title: Crafting
body: Crafting turns raw resources and gathered materials into gear and consumables. Instead of only buying equipment, you can build it, and crafted gear comes in tiers, from Common up through finer, master, and legendary grades that scale its stats.

Pick a recipe, check the cost and any special components it needs, and tap Craft. The panel shows exactly what a recipe requires next to what you own, and flags anything you are short on, so there is no guesswork. A successful craft drops the new item straight into your inventory, ready to equip.

Different crafts live in different places: weapon and armor recipes at the smiths, jewelry at the Jeweler, and potions and food via the village's consumable recipes. Some of the best recipes also call for special materials you earn from quests.
tips: If a component shows red, you are missing it; finish the quest or gather more.
Higher tiers cost more but multiply the gear's stats meaningfully.
Crafting and buying both feed the same inventory; use whichever is cheaper for you.

sections.title: Armory
body: Every weapon, armor set, and accessory carries a rarity, from Common and Uncommon up through Rare, Epic, and Legendary, and rarity scales the item's power. Weapons raise your damage, armor adds defense and bonus health, and accessories (rings and amulets) round out your build.

Many pieces have a level requirement and a class fit, so a weapon meant for one hero will not slot onto another. Gear is bought with the realm's resources, Wood, Iron, Food, and Crystals, so your economy directly feeds your power.

The Off-Hand slot is reserved for shields, keeping sword-and-board distinct from a heavier weapon. A shield is real armor, not decoration: every one carries a defense value, and the stronger shields ask for a higher hero level. Your total damage reduction from all your gear is capped, so a balanced set beats stacking a single slot.

The shops do not waste your time. The Forge and the Armorer show only what you can equip right now, for your class and at your level, a couple of choices per level, so the shelf grows as you do. The Jeweler shows accessories you have not reached yet, marked 'Requires Lv N'. Use the Gear Preview to see and compare a loadout on your hero before you commit.
tips: Check an item's level and class requirement before you save up for it.
Rarer is stronger, but a well-matched lower-rarity piece can beat an off-class higher one.
Defense reduces damage taken; bonus health gives you a bigger margin to heal through.
A shield adds real defense; the better ones need a higher level.
If the Forge shelf looks thin, level up -- it only stocks what you can wear.

sections.title: Leveling System
body: Your hero earns experience by defeating enemies. Cross a threshold and you level up instantly, with no break in the action. The XP bar on the HUD shows how close you are to the next level.

Each level makes you stronger in two ways. It raises your ability damage, so the same skills hit harder the more you fight, and it grants Wisdom, the points you spend in the Skill Tree. Early levels give a steady trickle of Wisdom, and later levels give a little more.
Because leveling pays out both raw power and Wisdom, every fight moves you forward twice: better numbers now, and a deeper skill build over time.
tips: Wisdom is your skill-point currency; spend it in the Skill Tree.
Leveling is automatic; just keep fighting.
Ability damage compounds with level, so your kit feels better the longer you play.

sections.title: Skill Tree
body: The Skill Tree is where you shape your hero. You spend Wisdom, earned from leveling and victories, to unlock nodes across four tiers, climbing from the basics up to powerful tier-four capstones. Higher tiers cost more Wisdom and sit behind the nodes below them.

Nodes come in two flavors. Skill nodes unlock a brand-new ability you can equip; stat nodes give permanent passive boosts like more damage, defense, or health. Alongside each hero's own tree there is a small pool of shared, universal nodes any hero can take.
This is the heart of your build. Want to lean into survival, burst, or sustain? The tree lets you commit, and unlocked abilities then go onto your skill bar (see Hot-Swap).
tips: Capstones are the tier-four payoffs; plan a path toward the one you want.
Unlocking a Skill node is step one; you still equip it on the skill bar to use it.
Stat nodes are quiet but always-on; do not overlook them.
The Knight's tree is fully wired for V1; other heroes follow as they come online.

sections.title: Hot-Swap Skill Bar
body: Your hero fights with two sets of abilities. The fixed class kit is your bread and butter: a basic attack that is always there, plus three signature abilities that define your class. That kit is your reliable baseline.

On top of that sits the hot-swap skill bar, a row of extra slots you fill yourself with abilities you unlock in the Skill Tree. This is how the tree pays off in combat: unlock a skill, then drag it into a slot to bring it into the fight.

You arrange the hot-swap bar out of combat. Drag a skill onto a slot, or move it between slots to taste, and it locks in for your next battle. In the fight, each slot has its own cooldown, so your custom kit plays right alongside your class signatures.
tips: Edit the bar between fights, not during one; assignments lock in for combat.
Only abilities you have unlocked in the Skill Tree can be slotted.
Mix your class kit with picked skills to cover damage, control, and sustain.
Empty slots show as a plus; drop a skill in to fill them.

sections.title: Arena Battles
body: When you close on an enemy in the world, the screen fades and you drop into an isolated battle arena, just your hero against a small family of foes, usually one to three, with a rare chance of a boss. There are no buildings in the way; it is a clean, open space to fight in.

Combat is real-time and built around movement. Kite, reposition, and time your abilities: open with your basic attack, weave in your signatures and hot-swap skills, and heal or control when the pressure spikes. Clear every enemy to win.

Win and you are rated with stars based on how fast and clean you fought: a quick finish earns three stars, a solid one two, and a win at any pace one. More stars multiply your rewards, XP, Wisdom, resources, and a better shot at gear. Then you warp back to where you were, the world a little safer.
tips: Three stars rewards the fastest clears; speed is paid in loot.
Keep moving; standing still in a real-time fight gets you hit.
Save a heal or a control skill for when a foe winds up a big hit.
Losing returns you to a safe spot, so a tough fight is never the end.
An Arena battle is your hero alone; Raids are where your trained troops fight.

sections.title: Defense Building
body: Back home, the realm strikes back in waves. Each wave opens with a prepare phase, a countdown to ready your defenses, then enemies march in from the gates toward the Heart of Elarion. You and your defenses hold them off; clear the wave to win, but let the Heart fall and the run ends.

The waves escalate in story and scale, from the first scattered Hollowed to orc warbands, troll brutes, and a dragon at the apex. Beating waves is also how your Echo workforce grows, so defending home directly feeds your economy.

Note on what is coming: the deeper base-building layer, freely placing and upgrading your own towers and walls, and converting cleared outposts into garrisoned bases that troops auto-defend, is a V2 feature still being built. For now, focus on holding the line with your hero as the waves test the village.
tips: Use the prepare countdown to position and ready yourself before enemies spawn.
Every five waves cleared unlocks another Echo for your workforce.
The Heart is what you are protecting; do not let enemies reach it.
Player-placed towers, walls, and garrison troops arrive in a later update.

sections.title: Echoes
body: An Echo is the awakened essence of one of the people the Heart of Elarion guards. The world tree remembers every soul it has kept, and when a new defender rises it wakes them to work beside you. They are not elementals and not pets -- they are the realm's remembered, lending a hand.

There are six in all: Aldwin, Elowen, Corvin, Bran, Doran and Maren. You begin with one, and every five waves you clear wakes another, up to the full roster of six. More Echoes means more gathered, so defending home directly feeds your economy.

Echoes gather whether you are playing or away. Their take pools in a shared silo that fills for a set number of hours and then stops. Tap Collect All when you return to bank it and restart the clock. That come-back-and-claim rhythm is the loop.
tips: You start with one Echo; clear five waves to wake the next.
Open an Echo's card to read who they were and what they favor.
Collect All banks the silo and any waiting building collectors together.
The silo stops once it is full, so come back before it tops out.
A stronger, healthier world tree means faster gathering, so keep pushing the dark back.

sections.title: Echoes: Affinity and Assignment
body: Every Echo has an affinity, the one resource they favor. Their card names it on the Favors line, and the matching chip in the picker is labelled 'best -- this Echo's calling'.

Affinity is a bonus, never a lock. You choose what each Echo gathers from the five chips on their card -- Wood, Iron, Food, Gold or Crystals -- and every chip is always tappable. Assign whatever your village is short of.
Set an Echo to the resource they favor and they bring in noticeably more of it. Set them anywhere else and they still work, just without the match bonus. Reassigning is free and takes effect at once.
tips: The picker lives on the Echo card: tap a resource chip to assign it.
The chip you are on now reads '(now)'; the favored one reads 'best'.
Affinity is spelled out in words, not signalled by color alone.
Chase what you are short of; the match bonus is a nudge, not a rule.

sections.title: Echoes: Synergy
body: Echoes work better in the right company. Three named pairs each lift ALL of your harvest while they are running: Provisions (Elowen and Aldwin), Forge (Doran and Maren), and Fortune (Corvin and Bran).

A pair only counts when you own both Echoes and both are assigned to the resource they favor. Each Echo card carries its pair line: either the synergy is ACTIVE, or it names the partner you still need.
Completing the roster pays again. Once all six Echoes are awake, everything they gather is lifted. Recruiting is the biggest single jump in your economy, bigger than levelling any one Echo.
tips: A pair needs BOTH members on their own favored resource.
Read the synergy line on the Echo card to see what is missing.
Owning more Echoes beats levelling one; recruit first.

sections.title: The Work Queue
body: Everything that takes time runs through one place: the Work Queue. Building and upgrading, training troops, and researching upgrades each get their own channel -- Builders, Training and Research -- and the channels never take slots from one another.
Each channel runs two jobs at once on a new village. Anything beyond that waits in line and starts on its own the moment a slot frees, so queueing more than you can run costs you nothing.

The Builders chip on the right of the screen is your at-a-glance readout: how many slots are busy and how long until the next one frees. Tap it to open the queue and see every running and waiting job.
tips: Builders, Training and Research are separate lines; a busy builder never blocks research.
Queued jobs start automatically -- you do not have to come back and press anything.
In the queue panel, '>' marks a running job and '-' marks a free slot.

sections.title: Raids
body: Raids are where your trained troops earn their keep. Open Journey, choose Raids, pick a target camp from the list, and you are taken straight there. There is no march; you arrive at the edge of the enemy camp.

On the field you deploy. Tap a troop tile to pick a unit, then tap the ground to drop one. Set a rally point to pull your troops toward a spot, or call a Retreat to pull the survivors out. Your hero fights alongside them.

A raid runs on a clock. When it ends you are scored up to three stars on how far you broke the camp, and paid resources to match. Raids stay closed until you have a Barracks and at least one trained troop.
tips: Build a Barracks and your first squad is free; with no troops the Raids card in Journey dims until you train more.
Retreat saves the survivors -- a bad raid does not have to be a total loss.
Raids are your troops; Arena battles are your hero alone.

sections.title: Heartfire
sections._note: WO-1415 (owner ruling 2026-09-05). Measured before this edit, grep -ci for 'heartfire' in this file returned ZERO: the mechanic that decides whether a player may raid at all (WO-1379 made Heartfire the ONE gate) was the one mechanic the guide never explained. The owner's own words from the felt-test on build 2026.09.05.356468: 'Heartfire is full, i dont understand as a new player what to do with that. No one in game has introduced me to heartfire.' THE SENTENCE 'each one sends you on a raid' IS THE OWNER'S RULING AND IS VERBATIM - it also lives as DeNelle.Core.State.HeartfireCharges.SpendSentence, is carried by the introduction beat (dialogues.json tut_ctx_heartfire) and is asserted in both files by HeartfireRegression PIN H, so the three surfaces cannot drift. The numbers (three charges, four hours) are the shipped defaults pinned by HeartfireRegression A0 against RemoteTunables.RaidHeartfireMaxChargesDefault / RaidHeartfireRegenSecondsDefault; they are tunable, so re-read them there before editing this copy.
body: Heartfire is the Heart of Elarion reaching past its own borders to keep an expedition alive, and each one sends you on a raid. You hold up to three. It is not a resource: nothing produces it, nothing sells it, nothing else can spend it, and no amount of anything will buy one.

One charge rekindles every four hours, whether the game is open or not, and the pool stacks to three - a day away from the game is never wasted. A charge is spent when you set out, so a raid costs one whether you win or lose. With none left the Heart is not ready to send you back yet, and the raid door tells you how long the wait is.
tips: The Heart plate on the left of the town screen reads Raids 3/3 (Heartfire); the marks beside it are your charges, filled or empty.
Heartfire is the only thing that decides WHEN you may raid - a camp you cleared an hour ago is not closed to you.
Sitting at three? Nothing accrues past the cap, so a full pool is a raid you have not taken yet.

sections.title: Troops
body: Your first Barracks raises a free squad of Footmen. That squad is the door to raids, not the whole army: the army holds more slots than the free squad fills, and every empty slot is a fighter you did not bring. Fill them from Manage, then Troops - training costs only time.

Levels change what a troop can do, not just how hard it hits. The Footman learns Sweeping Cut at L3, Warden's Roar at L5 and Champion's Combo at L7, and every troop has its own ladder. Upgrade from the same Troops card - the line under UPGRADE names the next unlock.
tips: The Raids card in Journey reads Army N / M until your ranks are full.
A locked camp on the raid grid already shows its walls and garrison - that is what your next wins buy.

sections.title: Dungeons
body: Dungeons are built room by room and entered from the world. The starter run is a loop: a corridor into a four-way junction, then a ring of rooms that bends back around to where you branched off.
Enemies belong to their rooms. They wake when you step into their space and settle back home if you leave, so you meet them a room at a time instead of dragging the whole floor behind you.
You can always leave. The way out is marked by a lit EXIT beacon: a beam of light and a plain EXIT sign you can pick out from across the room. Walk back to it whenever you have had enough.

Push to the deepest room and you will find a treasure cache. It asks before it opens and it pays once per run: torch materials, plus herbs for a Mending Salve. Clearing it the first time also teaches you the torch recipe.
tips: Follow the beam -- the EXIT beacon is always lit.
Fight room by room; enemies will not chain-pull across the floor.
The deepest room holds the cache, and it is worth the walk.
The torch itself is bound at the Healer's Cottage crafting pedestal.

sections.title: Saves and Sign-In
body: On Android the game opens on one simple choice: connect a wallet, or play as guest. Both take you straight in, and Play as Guest always works.
Your wallet is your save. Connect one and your progress is kept against it, so the same wallet on another device picks up where you left off. Guest progress stays on this device until you connect.
The wallet is used to sign in and nothing else: this build makes no purchases and moves no funds. You can start as a guest and connect later, and your progress comes with you.
tips: Play as Guest is never a dead end; you can connect a wallet afterwards.
Connect the SAME wallet on a second device to carry your village across.
Guest saves live on this device only -- connect before you change phones.

sections.title: Heart of Elarion
body: At the very center of the village stands the Heart of Elarion, the world tree and stone reliquary that everything else protects. It is the source of the realm's life force and the home the waves are trying to reach.

The Heart is more than a target. It releases the Echoes that gather for you, and it sets the village's tier, the gate that unlocks higher building upgrades as your home grows. As danger rises during a defense, the Heart even speaks, a living warning that a lane is breaking.
Keep the Heart standing and keep it strong. Driving enemies back feeds its life force, which heals the world and quickens your Echoes' harvest.
tips: If the Heart falls during a wave, the run is over; defend it above all.
The Heart's tier gates what your other buildings can upgrade to.
Listen to the Heart's voice in a defense; it flags trouble before you see it.

sections.title: Crystal Mine
body: The Crystal Mine taps the gem-sap that seeps from the Heart into the stone, producing Crystals, the realm's premium resource for shops, gear, and upgrades. It is one of your economy's cornerstones.
Build and upgrade it to raise its yield. As a resource building, its upgrade path is about level and output, more Crystals flowing in over time, so investing here pays for everything else.
Why bother? Crystals gate the rarer gear and the deeper upgrades, so a healthy mine quietly funds your whole build.
tips: Crystals are needed for rarer gear and many upgrades; keep the mine running.
Upgrading raises yield; treat it as compounding income.
Pair it with your other resource buildings for a balanced economy.

sections.title: Quarry
body: The Quarry cuts the bedrock the Heart wills up beneath your town, producing Stone for the realm. Stone is one of the core resources your Barracks spends to grow your army.
Like the other resource buildings, the Quarry upgrades along a yield path: each level produces more Stone over time. It keeps your Barracks climbing and your army growing.
A steady Quarry means you are never stalled on Stone when you want to train or upgrade.
tips: Stone pays for Barracks upgrades and the troops they unlock; do not let it run dry.
Upgrade the Quarry to keep pace with your spending.
Resource buildings work best upgraded together.

sections.title: Lumber Mill
body: The Lumber Mill cuts timber into planks, producing Wood, the most common building and crafting resource and the bones of your walls and gear. Its blade hums against the timber the green places of Elarion still spare.
Upgrade it along its yield path to bring in more Wood per cycle. Wood is also one of the things your Echoes harvest, so the Lumber Mill and your workforce both feed the same pile.
Plentiful Wood keeps crafting cheap and your defenses well supplied.
tips: Wood is your most-used resource; a strong Lumber Mill keeps everything affordable.
Echoes can gather Wood too, stacking with the mill's output.
Upgrade early so you are never short on the basics.

sections.title: Echo Hollow
body: The Echo Hollow is an ancient recess in the world tree's roots where the Echoes rest between their work, their presence a low hum in the stones. It is the home of your gathering spirits.

Think of the Hollow as the heart of your passive economy, the place tied to the Echo workforce that grows as you clear waves. It grounds the spirits that keep harvesting while you fight and while you are away.
A thriving Hollow means a thriving workforce, which means more resources flowing in for everything else you want to build.
tips: Your Echoes are tied to the Hollow; grow your workforce by clearing waves.
See the Echoes tab for how the harvest-and-Dump loop works.
More Echoes, more passive resources; this is the engine of your idle economy.

sections.title: Workshop
body: The Workshop is where the Folk make what the Keeper needs and ask nothing in return. It is the village's general crafting and production hall, hammer and forge working together.
Use it as a hub for turning your resources into useful goods. As your village tier rises at the Heart, the Workshop and its kin can be upgraded for better output.
A solid Workshop keeps the village self-sufficient, less buying, more making.
tips: Lean on the Workshop to craft from resources you already have.
Upgrades unlock as your village tier rises at the Heart.
Pair production buildings with strong resource buildings to keep them fed.

sections.title: Forge
body: The Forge is the smith's fire that never cools, where raw iron is beaten into plate the Hollowed cannot easily bite through. It is your weapons-and-gear smith: a place to both buy equipment and upgrade what you carry.

Step inside and you can shop for gear, sell what you have outgrown, and run the upgrade flow to improve your equipment. The Forge is one of the buildings that does double duty, a store and a smithy in one.
Coming back to the Forge as you level is how you keep your weapon matched to the fights ahead.
tips: The Forge both sells gear and upgrades it; use both flows.
Sell gear you have outgrown to fund the next tier.
Match your weapon's level and class requirement to your hero.

sections.title: Armorer
body: The Armorer is the realm's dedicated smith for protection, where the Folk shape iron into the plate that keeps you standing through a wave. Where the Forge leans toward your weapon, the Armorer is your place for armor.
Like the Forge, it both sells gear and runs an upgrade flow, so you can buy a fresh set and improve the one you wear. Better armor means more defense and more bonus health to heal through.
Visit the Armorer when fights start hitting harder than your current set can absorb.
tips: Upgrade armor when you are taking too much damage to heal through.
Defense and bonus health both come from your armor set.
The Armorer buys and sells gear, just like the Forge.

sections.title: Market
body: The Market is the village's trading floor, where you buy and sell goods. It is a shop building, your place to convert resources into the items you want and to offload what you do not need.
Drop in to browse what is for sale, pick up consumables and gear, and sell surplus back for resources. It keeps your inventory and your resource bins flowing in both directions.
A short trip to the Market is often the fastest way to fix a gap in your kit between fights.
tips: Sell surplus here to free up space and gain resources.
Stock up on consumables before a tough stretch.
Compare Market prices with crafting before you spend.

sections.title: Jeweler
body: The Jeweler specializes in the accessories that round out your build, the rings and amulets that fill your hero's two accessory slots. It is a shop, and the home of the realm's finer crafted trinkets.
Visit to buy accessories and to craft jewelry from your materials. Accessories add bonus health and other perks on top of your weapon and armor, the finishing touches on a loadout.
When your weapon and armor are solid, the Jeweler is where you squeeze out that extra edge.
tips: Accessories fill your Ring and Amulet slots; one of each.
The Jeweler both sells and crafts accessories.
Treat accessories as the polish on an already-strong build.

sections.title: Arcane Tower
body: The Arcane Tower was built by the first Keepers and holds the ward-stones that answer your call. It is the realm's most imposing structure, the tallest silhouette in the village and its sturdiest, with the most health of any building.

Unlike the resource and shop buildings, the Tower upgrades along a spells path: its own system of magical wards and powers, damage-over-time, area effects, and mana, that you research and improve. It is your magical backbone for the defense.
Invest in the Tower when you want the village itself to fight back with arcane power, not just your hero.
tips: The Tower upgrades spells, not resources; it is its own research track.
It is the toughest building, a strong anchor in your defenses.
Higher village tiers at the Heart unlock its deeper upgrades.
